competitors.title: Galileo Agent Control: Open Source Control Plane for AI Agents
key_points: Centralized layer for evaluating LLM and tool inputs/outputs during agent workflow execution
Blocks harmful content, prompt injection, PII leakage without requiring agent code changes
For developers: centralize safety logic and adapt to emerging threats without redeployment
For non-technical teams: configure and monitor agent safety without touching code
For organizations: reuse controls across agents with audit-ready traces
Single @control() decorator makes any function governable
Policies defined on server propagate to every connected agent in seconds

Gateway solutions blind to internal agent steps; framework-level guardrails require code changes per agent
Pluggable evaluator architecture: Galileo Luna, NVIDIA NeMo, AWS Bedrock, regex, custom evaluators all through same control plane
Launch partners: Cisco AI Defense, CrewAI, Strands Agents SDK, Glean, Rubrik, ServiceNow

competitors.title: OWASP ASI01: Mapping Every Agent Goal Hijack Variant to Detection and Defense (April 2026)
key_points: Seven variants of agent goal hijack: direct injection, indirect via RAG, indirect via external channels, multi-turn manipulation, goal-lock drift via scheduled prompts, cross-agent propagation, deceptive tool output injection
Most guardrails catch only variant 1 (direct injection) — remaining 6 go undetected
EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) in Microsoft 365 Copilot: zero-click prompt injection scoring 9.3 CVSS
Defense: injection detection on everything agent reads (not just user input), least privilege on tools, outbound allowlists
Luna-2 SLM detection in under 50ms per evaluation, combined with regex for known patterns

competitors.title: OWASP ASI02: When AI Agents Weaponize Their Own Tools (May 2026)
key_points: Seven attack patterns: tool poisoning via compromised definitions, indirect injection leading to tool pivot, over-privileged API access, internal query to external exfiltration, tool name impersonation, EDR bypass via tool chaining, approved tool misuse at scale
Taco Bell AI agent ordered 18,000 glasses of water — loop amplification pattern
Agent Control policies use three-part structure: scope (where), condition (what), action (what to do)
Pre-step validation, adaptive tool budgeting, output scanning as layered defenses
Six key Galileo metrics for ASI02: Prompt Injection, PII/CPNI, Context Adherence, Tool Selection Quality, Tool Error Rate, Agent Efficiency

angles: The three-layer guardrail architecture: Input Guard (prompt injection detection) → Execution Guardrail (tool-level policy enforcement via Agent Control) → Output Guard (PII/hallucination scanning via Protect) — and how Galileo implements all three in one platform
Open source vs proprietary guardrails: Agent Control (Apache 2.0) vs vendor-locked solutions — why enterprises are choosing open source for governance infrastructure to avoid vendor lock-in
OWASP ASI01-ASI10 as the compliance blueprint: how Galileo maps its 31 pre-built metrics to the full OWASP threat taxonomy, giving security teams an auditable trail for EU AI Act and GDPR compliance

The security team owns the controls, not developers: enterprise governance model where centralized security teams define policies on Agent Control server and developers just add @control() decorators — no code changes needed for policy updates
Luna-2 SLMs as the cost breakthrough: sub-200ms latency at ~97% lower cost than GPT-style judges enables always-on guardrailing that was previously too expensive for production scale

From gateway to step-level enforcement: why API proxy guardrails (blind to internal agent steps) and framework-native guardrails (require code changes per agent) both fail — and how Agent Control's @control() decorator at every decision boundary solves both problems

The seven variants of prompt injection most guardrails miss: most tools catch only direct injection; Galileo's Luna-2 detects indirect injection via RAG, multi-turn manipulation, cross-agent propagation, and deceptive tool output injection

Tool misuse as the #1 production failure: implementing tool-level guardrails with allowlists, permission scoping, argument validation, and adaptive tool budgeting — with real policy examples from banking, healthcare, and HR tech scenarios
